requirements.statement: A put option gives its holder the right to sell the underlying asset at the strike price on the expiry date (European: only at expiry).

places.quote: A **European option** gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy (a **call**) or sell (a **put**) an underlying asset at a fixed strike price $K$ on one date only, the expiry date $T$.

requirements.statement: The payoff of a long put at expiry is max(K - S_T, 0), where K is the strike and S_T is the stock price at expiry.

places.quote: \text{Put: } (K - S_T)^+ = \max(K - S_T,\,0)
\text{Put payoff} = (K - S_T)^+

requirements.statement: The buyer of an option pays the premium at time 0 and the writer (seller) receives it; the writer's cash flows are the exact opposite of the holder's (options are a zero-sum contract).

places.quote: A bull call spread costs money up front, while a bull put spread brings in a premium.
Selling a call must bring in at least \$4.02.

resolution.quote: A covered call is long the stock and short a call, with payoff $\min(S_T, K)$. It earns the premium
resolution.note: retagged Option Trading Strategy: the writer of a call earns the premium (the holder pays it); quote replaces the check's weaker spread quotes

requirements.statement: Profit on an option position is the payoff at expiry plus the premium paid (or received) accumulated with interest at the risk-free rate; it is a summary of the cash flows, not a separate cash flow.

places.quote: Profit is the payoff less the accumulated premium
\text{Profit} = \text{Payoff} - \text{Net premium}

requirements.statement: In the Black-Scholes framework, d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r - δ + 0.5σ²)T] / (σ√T), and d2 = d1 - σ√T.

places.quote: $d_1 = \dfrac{\ln(S/K) + (r - \delta + \sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}$
$$d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}$$

requirements.statement: The delta of a European put on a non-dividend-paying stock is -N(-d1), which equals N(d1) - 1 and is negative.

places.quote: $$\Delta_{P} = -e^{-\delta T} N(-d_1)$$
$N(d_1)$ for the call, $-N(-d_1)$ for the put.
A European put has $\Delta_p = e^{-qT}\left[N(d_1) - 1\right]$

requirements.statement: Delta is the change in an option's value per unit change in the stock price, and a position's delta is the number of options times the signed (long positive, short negative) per-option delta.

places.quote: $\Delta$ being the derivative's sensitivity to the asset price
The Greek of a portfolio is the sum of the Greeks of its positions, weighted by quantity.

requirements.statement: To delta-hedge an option position, take a stock position whose delta (number of shares) is the negative of the option position's delta, so the total delta is zero; a positive net option delta requires shorting shares and a negative one requires buying shares.

places.quote: A writer of the derivative holds $+\Delta$ shares per option sold (a call writer buys stock, a put writer shorts it)
The call's delta is $0.536$ and the put's is $-0.464$: a writer of the put hedges by shorting $0.464$ shares per option.
The first two blocks are **delta-neutral** and **gamma-neutral** conditions

requirements.statement: Insurable interest is a financial or legally recognized stake in the insured person or property, such that the policyholder would suffer a loss from the insured event, and it is required for a valid insurance contract.

places.quote: **Insurable interest** is a relationship to the subject of insurance — a property, a liability exposure, a person's life — such that the policyholder would suffer a genuine financial loss if the insured event occurred.

requirements.statement: Life insurance requires an insurable interest only at inception of the policy; the policy remains valid if the relationship (e.g., marriage) later ends.

places.quote: **When it must exist.** For property and liability cover, at the **time of loss**; for [[Life Insurance|life insurance]], at **inception** only — the policy stays valid if the relationship later ends.

requirements.statement: Property insurance requires an insurable interest at the time of loss, because it indemnifies a loss the insured actually suffers.

places.quote: **When it must exist.** For property and liability cover, at the **time of loss**; for [[Life Insurance|life insurance]], at **inception** only — the policy stays valid if the relationship later ends.

requirements.statement: A mere expectation of a future benefit (such as an expected inheritance) or an intention to buy property, with no ownership right or contract, is not an insurable interest.

resolution.quote: A mere expectancy is not insurable: a hope of inheriting property, or an intention to buy it, with no right to the property and no contract for it, gives the holder nothing a loss can take away.
resolution.note: Teaches that an expectancy (inheritance hope, intention to buy) with no right and no contract is not an insurable interest. Source: Cal. Ins. Code §283 (california.public.law); §281. Checked by a different agent from the writer.

requirements.statement: A buyer already bound by a contract of sale can have an insurable interest in property before the sale closes.

resolution.quote: A buyer already bound by a contract of sale is different: the contract is a right the loss would impair, so the buyer has an insurable interest before the sale closes and title passes.
resolution.note: Teaches that a buyer bound by a contract of sale has an insurable interest before closing. Source: FC&S (PropertyCasualty360, 13 Nov 2009) on Whitten v. Cincinnati Ins. Co., 544 N.E.2d 1169 (1989); Cal. Ins. Code §283 ('nor upon any valid contract for it'). Checked by a different agent from the writer.

requirements.statement: The insurable interest requirement exists to prevent wagering: a policy on a stranger's life by someone with no financial or family tie lacks insurable interest and is an unenforceable wager.

places.quote: **Void.** No interest at inception — the contract is a wager on the stranger's life, the abuse insurable-interest law exists to prevent.

requirements.statement: A defined benefit plan specifies the member's benefit by a formula (e.g., accrual rate × years of service × final average salary), independent of fund performance.

places.quote: A **Defined Benefit Plan** (DB plan) is a [[Retirement Plan]] that promises each member a pension set by a formula — usually an accrual rate $\alpha$ times years of service $n$ times a salary measure — and leaves the [[Plan Sponsor]] to contribute whatever it takes to fund that promise.
In a [[Defined Benefit Plan|defined benefit (DB)]] plan the benefit is set by formula from salary and service

requirements.statement: In a defined benefit plan the plan sponsor bears investment risk and longevity risk, because it must fund the promised benefits, so poor returns or longer lifetimes raise required sponsor contributions while members' pensions are unchanged.

places.quote: Risks — investment, [[Mortality|longevity]] and, for FAS, salary inflation — are the sponsor's; the member's pension does not move with the fund.
in DB, investment, [[Mortality|longevity]] and inflation risk sit with the sponsor; in DC they sit with the member.

in DB the sponsor bears investment, interest-rate, [[Mortality|longevity]] and salary risk, which surface as contribution volatility, balance-sheet liabilities under accounting standards, and cash demands in bad years.

requirements.statement: A defined contribution plan fixes the contribution rate (e.g., a percentage of payroll) and the member's benefit is whatever the account balance can provide, so members bear investment and longevity risk.

places.quote: a [[Defined Contribution Plan]] when the *contribution* is promised and the benefit is whatever the account buys

**The member bears the risks** a [[Defined Benefit Plan]] leaves with the [[Plan Sponsor]]: investment returns before retirement, annuity prices (interest rates and [[Mortality|longevity]]) at retirement, and — if no annuity is bought — outliving the account.

requirements.statement: In a life annuity pension, a member who lives longer receives the same annual benefit for more years, so the extra cost of longevity falls on the party guaranteeing the annuity rather than reducing the annual amount.

places.quote: A **Life Annuity** pays periodic benefits contingent on the survival of one or more lives.

**Longevity Risk** is the risk that people live longer than assumed, so that payments contingent on survival, such as [[Annuity Contract|annuities]] and defined benefit [[Pension|pensions]], last longer and cost more than the provider set aside.

requirements.statement: In a defined contribution plan the contribution (e.g., a percentage of salary) is fixed and the benefit is not; the benefit is whatever the accumulated account balance provides at retirement.

places.quote: The contribution is promised; the benefit is not.
a [[Defined Contribution Plan]] when the *contribution* is promised and the benefit is whatever the account buys,

requirements.statement: The annual pension from a DC account equals the account balance at retirement divided by the annuity price per 1 of annual income at that time.

In a DC plan the member bears the investment and annuity-pricing risk: a projected annuity price or replacement ratio in an illustration is not guaranteed, and lower interest rates or improved mortality raise the annuity price at retirement and reduce the pension.

places.quote: **The member bears the risks** a [[Defined Benefit Plan]] leaves with the [[Plan Sponsor]]: investment returns before retirement, annuity prices (interest rates and [[Mortality|longevity]]) at retirement, and — if no annuity is bought — outliving the account.
**Who bears the risk** is what separates the types: in DB, investment, [[Mortality|longevity]] and inflation risk sit with the sponsor; in DC they sit with the member.
At retirement, low interest rates raise the price of an annuity, and the order of returns matters most just after withdrawals begin, which is sequence-of-returns risk.

requirements.statement: Value at risk (VaR) at security level p is the p-th percentile of the loss distribution, the value x with F(x) = p.

places.quote: **Value at Risk** is the lower $p$-quantile of the loss ([[Percentile]]).

The **Percentile** (or quantile) $x_p$ of a [[Random Variable]] $X$ is the smallest value at which the [[Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)|CDF]] reaches $p$, so at least a proportion $p$ of the distribution lies at or below it.

requirements.statement: Tail value at risk (TVaR) at security level p is the expected loss given that the loss exceeds VaR at p, E[X | X > VaR_p].

places.quote: The **conditional tail expectation** $E[X \mid X \geq \text{VaR}_p]$ equals TVaR for a continuous loss but not when there is a probability mass at $\text{VaR}_p$.

requirements.statement: For a continuous loss, TVaR_p equals VaR_p plus the mean excess loss (mean residual life) evaluated at VaR_p, i.e. TVaR_p = VaR_p + e(VaR_p).

places.quote: **Tail Value at Risk** averages the worst $1-p$ of outcomes; for any distribution $\text{TVaR}_p = \text{VaR}_p + E[(X - \text{VaR}_p)^+]/(1-p)$.
The cost per loss is $E[(X - d)_+] = e_X(d)\,S_X(d)$, which is the [[Payment Random Variable|per-loss]] counterpart of this per-payment quantity.

requirements.statement: The two-parameter Pareto distribution has survival function S(x) = (θ/(x+θ))^α, which can be set equal to 1−p and inverted to get percentiles.

places.quote: $$F(x) = 1 - \left(\frac{\theta}{x + \theta}\right)^{\alpha}$$
When $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing, it is the value that solves $F(x_p) = p$, found by inverting the CDF.

requirements.statement: For a two-parameter Pareto with α > 1, the mean excess loss at d is e(d) = (d + θ)/(α − 1).

places.quote: So the expected payment per payment is $E[X - d \mid X > d] = \frac{\theta + d}{\alpha - 1}$, which grows with $d$.

The [[Pareto Distribution|Pareto]] has $e_X(d) = (d + \theta)/(\alpha - 1)$ for $\alpha > 1$, which increases linearly, and a uniform loss on $(0, \omega)$ has $e_X(d) = (\omega - d)/2$, which decreases to zero.

requirements.statement: Adverse selection in insurance is the tendency of people with higher-than-average risk (e.g., higher mortality for death benefits) to seek or buy coverage, and underwriting is the process of classifying applicants to mitigate it.

places.quote: It is the insurer's defence against [[Adverse Selection|adverse selection]]: pricing assumes an average risk in each class, and underwriting is what keeps the risks in the class average.

**Adverse Selection** is the tendency for those who know they are worse-than-average risks to buy more insurance, and better-than-average risks to buy less, when the insurer cannot distinguish between them.

requirements.statement: Products that pay benefits on death (e.g., life insurance) need underwriting because higher-than-expected mortality raises the actuarial present value of benefits.

places.quote: Dropping full underwriting saves $\$300$ but adds about $\$844$ of expected claims per policy, so at this face amount full underwriting pays for itself.
Mortality assumptions drive every [[Life Insurance|life insurance]] and [[Life Annuity|annuity]] value: higher mortality raises insurance costs and lowers annuity costs.

requirements.statement: Products that pay benefits only while the insured survives (single premium immediate annuities, pure endowments) do not need underwriting against adverse selection, since higher-than-expected mortality reduces the actuarial present value of benefits and benefits the insurer.

places.quote: ${}_nE_x$ falls when the interest rate rises and rises when mortality is lighter. That is the opposite of a death benefit's response to mortality, which is why survival benefits carry longevity risk.
Mortality assumptions drive every [[Life Insurance|life insurance]] and [[Life Annuity|annuity]] value: higher mortality raises insurance costs and lowers annuity costs.

requirements.statement: The distribution method affects the level of underwriting; for example, direct-marketed low face amount products may have very limited underwriting, with extra mortality assumed and partly offset by lower selling expenses.

places.quote: Direct response and online sales reach customers without an agent, usually for simple term products with simplified or accelerated [[Underwriting|underwriting]].

requirements.statement: Underwriting may classify an applicant as a rated (substandard) life when a hazardous occupation or hobby increases expected mortality.

places.quote: **Extra Risk** is mortality heavier than the standard basis, carried by a life who does not meet the insurer's standard [[Underwriting|underwriting]] criteria because of a medical impairment, a hazardous occupation or a dangerous pastime.

requirements.statement: Life insurance products and their risk management have become more complex over recent decades because policyholders are more sophisticated, competition among insurers has increased, and computational power has grown.
requirements.concept: Evolution of Life Insurance Products and Risk Management

requirements.statement: Modern life insurance risk management has become more complex through the use of more advanced risk management techniques.
requirements.concept: Evolution of Life Insurance Products and Risk Management

places.quote: The environment it works in has moved from buying insurance for pure loss exposures toward [[Enterprise Risk Management|enterprise risk management]], which treats every source of risk, with its upside as well as its downside, as one portfolio.

requirements.statement: Modern life insurance products increasingly combine savings elements with protection elements rather than separating them, as seen in products like universal life and variable annuities.
requirements.concept: Evolution of Life Insurance Products and Risk Management

places.quote: and policies with account values such as [[Universal Life Insurance|universal life]] and equity-linked contracts

requirements.statement: A variable annuity is a modern insurance contract whose benefits are linked to the performance of an underlying investment fund, usually with guaranteed minimum benefits such as a minimum return or minimum death benefit.

places.quote: It may be **immediate** (income starts at once) or **deferred** (an accumulation phase first), and **fixed** (guaranteed amounts) or **variable** (amounts linked to a fund, often with guarantees).
Such contracts are sold as variable annuities in the United States, segregated fund contracts in Canada and unit-linked contracts in the United Kingdom.

requirements.statement: Traditional contracts such as term life, endowment insurance and reversionary annuities have benefits that are fixed or defined by the contract and not linked to an investment fund's performance.

places.quote: | [[Endowment Insurance]] | Sum insured on death within $n$ years or on survival to $n$ | Interest |
**Term Life Insurance** pays a sum insured if the insured dies within a fixed term of $n$ years, and nothing if the insured survives the term.

requirements.statement: Universal life insurance is a flexible-premium contract with an account value credited with interest, rather than a benefit linked directly to the performance of an investment fund.

places.quote: **Universal Life Insurance** (UL) is a flexible-premium permanent [[Life Insurance|life insurance]] policy built on a transparent **account value**: premiums are credited to the account, expense and cost-of-insurance charges are deducted, and interest is credited at a declared rate.
| [[Universal Life Insurance]] | Death benefit plus an account value credited with interest | Interest, lapse |

requirements.statement: Disability income insurance replaces a portion of the insured's salary when illness or injury prevents the insured from working, typically with benefits ceasing at retirement age.

places.quote: replaces part of a person's earned income while sickness or injury keeps the insured from working.
| Disability income insurance | Income while the insured is sick | Morbidity, recovery |

requirements.statement: Long-term care insurance pays benefits when the insured cannot perform a specified number of activities of daily living or has cognitive impairment, covering care costs rather than replacing income.

places.quote: pays for the personal care a person needs when they can no longer look after themselves because of chronic illness, frailty or cognitive decline, in a nursing facility, an assisted living facility or at home.
| Long-term care insurance | Care costs while the insured cannot live independently | Morbidity, longevity |

requirements.statement: Critical illness insurance pays a lump-sum benefit on diagnosis of a specified serious illness (e.g., cancer, heart attack), regardless of ability to work.

places.quote: pays a lump sum when the insured is first diagnosed with one of the serious conditions the policy lists, such as cancer, heart attack or stroke
| Critical illness insurance | Lump sum on diagnosis of a listed illness | Morbidity |

requirements.statement: Term life insurance pays a death benefit only if the insured dies within the policy term, and a single premium immediate annuity pays periodic income starting immediately in exchange for a single premium; neither is triggered by sickness.

places.quote: | [[Life Annuity]] | Income while the annuitant is alive | Longevity, interest |
pays a sum insured if the insured dies within a fixed term of $n$ years, and nothing if the insured survives the term.

requirements.statement: A mixed distribution arises when a common random factor (here, whether the vaccine is available) affects all lives, so the lives are independent only conditional on the scenario and not unconditionally; the overall distribution is a probability-weighted mixture of the conditional distributions.

places.quote: A **Mixture Distribution** describes a variable $X$ drawn from a population made of subpopulations with different distributions: first a subpopulation is chosen at random, then $X$ is drawn from it.

requirements.statement: Conditional variance formula (law of total variance): Var(S) = E[Var(S|A)] + Var(E[S|A]); equivalently, compute E(S) and E(S^2) as probability-weighted averages over scenarios and use Var(S) = E(S^2) - E(S)^2.

requirements.statement: The variance of a two-point random variable taking one value with probability p and another with probability 1-p is p(1-p) times the squared difference between the values.

the two parts are mutually exclusive, so the covariance is $-A^1\,{}_nE_x$ and the second moments add instead.

A select-and-ultimate mortality table uses select mortality rates q_[x]+k for durations within the select period and ultimate rates q_{x+k} afterward, so a select life's survival and insurance values combine select-period rates with ultimate rates after the select period.

places.quote: A table therefore gives select rates $q_{[x]+t}$ for durations within the select period and ultimate rates $q_{x+t}$ after it, and each select column should grade smoothly into the ultimate column.

resolution.quote: Square brackets mark the age at selection, so $q_{[x]+t}$ is the mortality rate at age $x+t$ for a life selected (underwritten) at age $x$, $t$ years ago. After the select period ends the brackets drop and the ultimate rate $q_{x+t}$ applies.
resolution.note: Select-and-ultimate structure (select rates within the select period, ultimate rates by attained age after it) is taught on Standard Actuarial Notation, a page on FAM's syllabus; the check quoted only Mortality Table Construction (ILA-101).

The expense policy value is the actuarial present value of future expenses minus the actuarial present value of future expense premiums, where the expense premium is the portion of the gross premium that covers expenses (gross premium minus net premium).

The level expense premium equals the present value of expenses (first-year commission and administrative expenses plus renewal expenses times the annuity-due factor) divided by the life annuity-due factor at issue.
The gross premium policy value equals the net premium policy value plus the expense policy value, and the expense premium equals the gross premium minus the net premium.

A death in year 20 is paid at the same time as the maturity benefit, so it costs no more.

requirements.statement: The survival probability equals one minus the mortality probability (p_x = 1 - q_x), and the death benefit for the year in question is determined from the given benefit schedule (death in year k pays the amount for year k).

places.quote: its EPV is $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} b_{k+1}\,v^{k+1}\,{}_kp_x\,q_{x+k}$ for a benefit $b_{k+1}$ on death in year $k+1$.

The APV of insurance at an older age can be used as a terminal value after a finite sequence of explicit years: the benefit from that later age onward is valued as A at that age, discounted and weighted by the probability of surviving to it (recursive relationship A_x = v q_x + v p_x A_{x+1}).

The APV of a limited-payment premium stream is the premium times a temporary annuity-due, summing v^k times k-year survival probability only over the premium payment period, with no payments after the premium period ends.

places.quote: If the loss $X$ is less than or equal to the deductible $d$, the insurer pays nothing; above $d$ it pays the excess $X - d$

requirements.statement: For a continuous random variable, P(Y < y) = 1 − P(Y ≥ y), and P(X ≥ x) = 1 − F(x), so P(X ≥ x) = 1 − F(x) with no point-mass adjustment.

places.quote: For a nonnegative loss with survival function $S(x) = 1 - F(x)$

requirements.statement: A per-loss ordinary deductible d reduces each loss to max(X - d, 0), so the insurer pays nothing on losses below d and pays the loss minus d on losses above d.

places.quote: If the loss $X$ is less than or equal to the deductible $d$, the insurer pays nothing; above $d$ it pays the excess $X - d$

requirements.statement: From grouped loss data, compute total losses paid under a deductible d by taking total ground-up losses, removing the losses in layers entirely below d, and subtracting d times the number of claims exceeding d.

places.quote: For a discrete loss with probability function $p(x)$, the payment sums over the loss amounts above $d$, and the retained part takes each amount below $d$ at its value and every other at $d$.

requirements.statement: Loss cost is proportional to expected insurer payments, so the percentage reduction in loss costs from changing deductibles equals the percentage reduction in total paid losses with the same exposure and claim frequency.

places.quote: The LER is the bridge from a full-coverage rate to a deductible rate: multiply the full-coverage loss cost by $(1 - \text{LER})$ to get the loss cost net of the deductible.
$$\text{Loss Cost} = \frac{E[\text{Losses}]}{\text{Exposure}}$$

requirements.statement: The percentage reduction in loss cost from moving from deductible d1 to a higher deductible d2 is (payments at d1 - payments at d2) / payments at d1.

resolution.note: arithmetic: a percentage reduction is (old - new)/old; the deductible loss costs themselves are taught.

requirements.statement: On-level premium is the premium that would have been earned in a past period had the current rate level been in effect throughout, obtained by dividing the earned premium by the average rate level during the period and multiplying by the current rate level.

places.quote: **On-Level Premium** is historical earned premium restated as though every policy had been written at the rate level currently in effect.

requirements.statement: The parallelogram method for on-level factors: draw the calendar-year square with policy term as the side, plot rate change dates as diagonal lines, and compute the area of each rate-level region within the calendar year.

places.quote: A calendar year is a unit square: time across, fraction of the policy term earned up. A rate change for policies written on or after a date is a **diagonal** line whose slope is set by the term (steeper for six-month policies).
A rate change effective on date $d$ enters as a diagonal line; each region's **area** is the share of the year's earned premium written at that rate level.

requirements.statement: With one-year policies and uniformly distributed issues, a rate change affects earned premium gradually over a year, so the calendar-year average rate level is the area-weighted average of the cumulative rate relativities, with weights equal to each region's share of the calendar-year area.

places.quote: $I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change), $I_{\text{current}}$ the latest index — even if the change came after the experience period — and $A_{Y,k}$ the share (area) of year $Y$'s earned premium written at level $k$.
The *average* index for a year is the earned-premium-weighted blend of the levels in force during that year.

requirements.statement: Cumulative rate level indices are found by compounding successive rate changes multiplicatively (each change multiplies the prior level by 1 plus the change), measured relative to a chosen base level.

places.quote: $I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change), $I_{\text{current}}$ the latest index — even if the change came after the experience period — and $A_{Y,k}$ the share (area) of year $Y$'s earned premium written at level $k$.
Rate level indices **compound**: successive changes of $+8\%$ and $+5\%$ give a cumulative index of $1.08 \times 1.05 = 1.134$, not $1.13$.

requirements.statement: Rate changes before the earliest period's coverage affect no earned premium in the period (all premium is at the already-established level), so only changes whose parallelogram lines cut through the calendar year need area computations.

places.quote: CY 2025 needs none at all, since every policy written before $4/1/2024$ expired by $10/1/2024$.

requirements.statement: In the loss ratio method, the indicated rate change is the (weighted) projected ultimate loss ratio divided by the permissible loss ratio, minus 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1 \quad \text{(all-variable form)}$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Projected ultimate losses are obtained by multiplying reported losses by the loss development factor to ultimate and by the loss trend factor raised to the number of trend years.

places.quote: The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).
$$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: The loss trend period runs from the average accident date of the experience period to the average accident date of the period the new rates will be in effect.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: For one-year policies written uniformly, rates in effect for one year starting on date D produce accident dates spanning two years, with average accident date one year after D.

places.quote: The first policy is exposed $7/1/2025$–$6/30/2026$ and the last $7/1/2026$–$6/30/2027$, so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: For accident-year data with uniformly written one-year policies, the average accident date of the accident year is its midpoint (July 1).

places.quote: Accident year $2023$ runs $1/1$–$12/31/2023$; with losses occurring uniformly, its average loss date is $7/1/2023$.

requirements.statement: Loss ratios for each year are computed as projected ultimate losses divided by earned premium at current rates, and are combined using the given credibility/weights into a weighted average.

places.quote: Weighting across years in the experience period is a judgment: many companies sum projected losses and premium across all years, which weights each year's loss ratio by its premium; others select weights, often giving more to the most recent years.
$$\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}$$

requirements.statement: The on-level factor is the current rate level divided by the average rate level in effect during the period of interest, and it multiplies historical earned premium to restate it at current rates.
requirements.concept: On-Level Premium (Extension of Exposures / Parallelogram Method)

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Average index for the year}}$$
$$\text{On-Level Premium} = \text{Historical EP} \times \text{On-Level Factor}$$
$$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the historical period}}$$

requirements.statement: In the parallelogram method, the average rate level for a calendar year is the area-weighted average of the cumulative rate levels, where each rate level is weighted by the share of the year's square (policy-date vs. calendar-time) falling in that level region.

places.quote: each region's **area** is the share of the year's earned premium written at that rate level.

**Werner's six steps:** date the changes and form rate level groups; find each group's area in each year; build cumulative indices; take the area-weighted average index; divide it into the current index; apply the factor to the year's earned premium.

requirements.statement: With policies written uniformly and a given term, the line for a rate change date on the policy-issue/time diagram is a diagonal, so policies issued before the change are earned at the old rate until term-length after the change, which produces triangular regions in the calendar-year square.

places.quote: A rate change for policies written on or after a date is a **diagonal** line whose slope is set by the term (steeper for six-month policies).
a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$

requirements.statement: Cumulative rate level indices are obtained by multiplying successive rate change factors (1 + percentage change) together.

places.quote: $I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change)
Rate level indices **compound**: successive changes of $+8\%$ and $+5\%$ give a cumulative index of $1.08 \times 1.05 = 1.134$, not $1.13$.

requirements.statement: A rate change whose effect has not fully earned into the year (e.g., a change whose policies are still in force from earlier) affects calendar-year earned premium only for the portion of the year's area its policies cover; a rate change that occurs before the year's earning period begins affects the year only via policies issued after the change, and the current-level factor uses the most recent rate level.

places.quote: CY 2025 needs none at all, since every policy written before $4/1/2024$ expired by $10/1/2024$.
Calendar year $2025$ would be fully at the new level, with an on-level factor of $1.000$.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson reserve equals the expected ultimate loss (earned premium times expected loss ratio) multiplied by the percent unreported/unpaid, 1 - 1/CDF.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The volume-weighted average age-to-age development factor for a period is the sum of cumulative losses at the later age divided by the sum of cumulative losses at the earlier age, using only accident years that have both values.

places.quote: - **Volume-weighted average**: $\Sigma(\text{col }n{+}1) / \Sigma(\text{col }n)$ — gives more credibility to larger accident years; the standard default selection
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor (to ultimate) is found by multiplying the successive age-to-age factors from the current age through the last development age, with a tail factor of 1.0 if there is no development beyond the last age.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete — and it is the wrong one for any casualty line.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: An accident year whose losses are fully developed (latest age at the final development age with no further development) has a CDF of 1 and therefore a zero reserve.

places.quote: The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.
A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete — and it is the wrong one for any casualty line.

requirements.statement: The indicated loss reserve is the ultimate loss estimate minus losses paid to date, and the total reserve is the sum of the reserves across accident years.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = U_{\text{AY}} - C_{\text{AY},\,n}$$

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) development factor for a given development period is the ratio of cumulative paid losses at the later age to cumulative paid losses at the earlier age for the same accident year.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n{+}1} = \frac{\text{Losses at age }n{+}1}{\text{Losses at age }n}$$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: An n-year arithmetic average development factor is the simple average of the individual age-to-age factors from the most recent n accident years available for that development period (using fewer if fewer exist).

places.quote: **Latest-$k$-year average**: uses only the most recent $k$ accident years — reduces the influence of older, potentially unrepresentative data
**Latest $k$-year** average (volume-weighted or simple) — responsive to a genuine change in the pattern, at the cost of credibility.

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate for an age is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from that age through the end of the triangle, with a tail factor (1 if none) at the end.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The expected percentage of ultimate losses still unreported or unpaid at a given age equals 1 minus 1/CDF, where CDF is the cumulative development factor to ultimate.

places.quote: $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson reserve for an accident year equals earned premium times the expected loss ratio times (1 - 1/CDF), i.e., the a priori expected ultimate loss times the expected percentage unpaid.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The total loss reserve is the sum of the accident-year reserves; an accident year already at the final development age has a zero reserve under the method since its CDF is 1.
The Bornhuetter-Ferguson reserve (IBNR) for an accident year equals expected ultimate losses times (1 - 1/CDF), i.e., expected losses times the percentage not yet reported.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Expected losses for an accident year equal earned premium times the expected loss ratio (a priori ELR).

places.quote: $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
$$U = \text{ELR} \times \text{Earned Premium}$$

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor (CDF) to ultimate for an accident year is the product of the age-to-age factors from its current age through ultimate.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: As of a valuation date, each successive accident year is one development period younger: at Dec 31 of CY3, AY1 is at 36 months, AY2 at 24 months, and AY3 at 12 months, which determines which age-to-age factors apply to each year.

places.quote: **Development Triangle** is the fundamental data structure of reserving: amounts arranged with **cohorts as rows** (usually [[Accident Year|accident years]]), **maturities as columns** (age in months since the start of the cohort), and **valuation dates as diagonals**.
The triangle is triangular because a $2024$ accident year cannot yet have a $36$-month valuation.

requirements.statement: The total IBNR reserve is the sum of the BF reserves across all accident years.
A catastrophe reinsurance layer written as 'x% of L excess of R' means the reinsurer pays x% of the portion of the loss falling between R and R+L, with the layer capped at L.

places.quote: is the slice of each loss between an attachment point $a$ and an exhaustion point $b = a + l$
the reinsurer pays the part of each loss — per risk or per occurrence — above the cedant's retention $R$ (the attachment point), up to a limit $L$.

requirements.statement: To find the reinsurer's payment on a layered treaty, apply each layer to the loss within its attachment and limit (min(loss, R+L) minus R, floored at zero), then multiply by the layer's reinsurer share percentage.

places.quote: $$Y = \min\left(\max(X - R,\, 0),\; L\right)$$
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{XS}} = \min\left(\max(X - R,\,0),\; L\right)$$

requirements.statement: The primary insurer's retained loss equals the retention plus the unreinsured share (1 minus the reinsurer's percentage) of each layer's loss, plus any loss above the top of the highest layer.

places.quote: $$\text{Net} = \text{Gross} - \text{Ceded}$$
Layers stack: the layers of a tower add up to the ground-up loss.
$$\text{Net} = \text{Gross} - \text{Ceded}$$

requirements.statement: An increased limits factor (ILF) at limit L is the ratio of expected loss at limit L to expected loss at the basic limit, i.e. E(X∧L)/E(X∧basic limit).

places.quote: $$\text{ILF}(L) = \frac{E[X \wedge L]}{E[X \wedge B]}$$
the increased limit factor for limit $H$ over basic limit $B$ is $\text{ILF}(H) = \text{LAS}(H)/\text{LAS}(B)$

requirements.statement: The expected loss in a layer from a to b equals E(X∧b) − E(X∧a), the difference of limited expected values.

places.quote: $$E[Y] = E[X \wedge (R + L)] - E[X \wedge R]$$
$$E\left[X_{(a,b]}\right] = E[X \wedge b] - E[X \wedge a]$$

requirements.statement: The proportion of total losses (capped at the policy limit) falling in a layer is the difference of ILFs at the layer's upper and lower limits divided by the ILF at the policy limit.

places.quote: In [[Increased Limits|ILF]] form, it is the basic-limits loss cost $\times\,[\text{ILF}(b) - \text{ILF}(a)]$.
For a limit above the top of the layer the share is the ILF at the top of the layer minus the ILF at the attachment point, divided by the ILF at the limit.

requirements.statement: A layer described as X in excess of Y has upper limit X+Y and lower limit Y, so a layer of 300,000 excess of 100,000 spans 100,000 to 400,000.

places.quote: the slice of each loss between an attachment point $a$ and an exhaustion point $b = a + l$, written "$l$ xs $a$"

requirements.statement: Expected losses equal the expected loss ratio times premium.

places.quote: In both cases the factor multiplies subject premium times the expected loss ratio.
Premium at a limit times the expected loss ratio estimates the expected losses of the policies at that limit

requirements.statement: In exponential trend (log-linear) projection, the trended loss cost equals the historical loss cost times e raised to the slope of the fitted line on log losses times the number of years between the historical period's average accident date and the future average accident date.

places.quote: The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: The slope of a straight line fitted to the natural log of loss costs is the continuously compounded annual trend rate, so e raised to the slope gives one plus the annual trend.

places.quote: $b$ is the [[Linear Regression|least-squares]] slope of $\ln y_t$ on $t$: $b = \sum (t - \bar{t})(\ln y_t - \overline{\ln y}) \big/ \sum (t - \bar{t})^2$. With $t$ in years, $\hat{T}$ is the annual trend

requirements.statement: Policies written over a one-year period with one-year terms have losses occurring over two years, so the average accident date of the new policies is one year after the rate effective date (midpoint of the written period plus half the policy term).

places.quote: Policies are written between $7/1/2025$ and $6/30/2026$; each provides coverage for a year after it is written.
for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.

requirements.statement: An accident year covering a calendar year has an average accident date at its midpoint (July 1, or about mid-year), which is used to measure the trending period to the future average accident date.

places.quote: The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)
Accident year $2023$ runs $1/1$–$12/31/2023$; with losses occurring uniformly, its average loss date is $7/1/2023$.

requirements.statement: The loss elimination ratio for an ordinary deductible d is the fraction of expected losses eliminated by the deductible, LER(d) = E[X ∧ d] / E[X].

places.quote: **Loss Elimination Ratio** (LER) is the proportion of ground-up losses removed by a deductible — the share of expected loss that the insured retains rather than transfers.

requirements.statement: Monotonicity requires that if X <= Y with certainty, then rho(X) <= rho(Y).

places.quote: *monotone*: $X \leq Y \Rightarrow \rho(X) \leq \rho(Y)$

requirements.statement: Positive homogeneity requires that rho(cX) = c*rho(X) for any constant c > 0.

requirements.statement: Translation invariance requires that rho(X + c) = rho(X) + c for any constant c.

places.quote: *translation invariant*: $\rho(X + c) = \rho(X) + c$

requirements.statement: Expectation is linear: E(X+Y) = E(X) + E(Y), E(cX) = cE(X), E(X+c) = E(X) + c, and X <= Y implies E(X) <= E(Y).

requirements.statement: In a one-period binomial model for a non-dividend-paying stock, the risk-neutral probability of an up move is p* = (e^{rh} - d)/(u - d), and the probability of a down move is 1 - p*.

places.quote: p^* = \frac{e^{(r - \delta)h} - d}{u - d}
p^* = \frac{e^{(r-\delta)h} - d}{u - d}

requirements.statement: The price of a European option in a binomial model equals the risk-free discounted expected payoff under risk-neutral probabilities: C = e^{-rh}[p* C_u + (1-p*) C_d].

places.quote: C = e^{-rh}\left[p^*C_u + (1 - p^*)\,C_d\right]
V_0 = e^{-rT}\, E^{\mathbb{Q}}\!\left[V_T\right]

requirements.statement: The payoff of a European put option at expiration is max(K - S_T, 0), where K is the strike price and S_T is the stock price at expiration.

places.quote: \text{Put payoff} = (K - S_T)^+
\text{Put: } (K - S_T)^+ = \max(K - S_T,\,0)

requirements.statement: In a one-period binomial model the stock price at the end of the period is either uS (up) or dS (down), so the put payoff is positive only in states where the stock ends below the strike.

places.quote: the price of the underlying asset either rises by a factor $u$ or falls by a factor $d$
A call is in the money when $S > K$, at the money when $S = K$ and out of the money when $S < K$, and a put is the reverse.

requirements.statement: Put-call parity for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock: C - P = S_0 - K e^{-rT}, where C and P are the call and put prices with strike K and expiration T, and r is the continuously compounded risk-free rate.

places.quote: $$C - P = S_0 e^{-\delta T} - K e^{-rT}$$
Call and put satisfy [[Put-Call Parity|put-call parity]], $c - p = S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$, which is a quick check on any pair of prices

requirements.statement: Put-call parity holds for every strike on the same underlying stock and expiration, so the stock price implied by one strike's call and put prices can be used with parity at another strike.

places.quote: the no-arbitrage identity linking a European call $C$ and a European put $P$ on the same underlying, with the same strike $K$ and expiry $T$
$$C - P = S_0 e^{-\delta T} - K e^{-rT}$$
Call and put satisfy [[Put-Call Parity|put-call parity]], $c - p = S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$, which is a quick check on any pair of prices

requirements.statement: A risk measure has the monotonicity property if, whenever X ≤ Y for all possible outcomes, then ρ(X) ≤ ρ(Y).

places.quote: *monotone*: $X \leq Y \Rightarrow \rho(X) \leq \rho(Y)$

requirements.statement: The variance of a random variable is Var(X) = E[X^2] − (E[X])^2, and the standard deviation is its square root.

places.quote: The second form $E[X^2] - \mu^2$ is the one to use in practice — it needs only two moments and avoids expanding a square.

requirements.statement: A constant random variable has variance and standard deviation equal to zero, so a standard-deviation-loaded risk measure of a constant equals the constant.

places.quote: The standard deviation principle fails monotonicity (with $k = 2$, a 50/50 chance of $0$ or $10$ scores $15$ — more than a certain loss of $10$)
$\text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\,\text{Var}(X)$ and $\text{SD}(aX + b) = |a|\,\text{SD}(X)$ — a shift $b$ moves the distribution without changing its spread.

requirements.statement: The standard deviation risk measure is ρ(X) = E[X] + kσ_X, the mean plus k times the standard deviation.

places.quote: the standard deviation principle $E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$
*standard deviation*: $P = E[X] + k\,\sigma(X)$

requirements.statement: In a binomial tree with continuously compounded risk-free rate r and period length h, the risk-neutral probability of an up move is p* = (e^{rh} - d)/(u - d), which can be rearranged to solve for d given p*, u and r.

places.quote: $$p^* = \frac{e^{(r - \delta)h} - d}{u - d}$$
$$p^* = \frac{e^{(r-\delta)h} - d}{u - d}$$

requirements.statement: Stock prices at each node of a recombining binomial tree are S0 * u^k * d^(n-k), so the up-down and down-up paths give the same price.

places.quote: Terminal prices are $S_{uu} = 66.125$, $S_{ud} = 51.75$, $S_{dd} = 40.50$, with put payoffs $0$, $2.25$ and $13.50$.

requirements.statement: The price of a European option in a multi-period binomial tree is the discounted expected payoff under risk-neutral probabilities: e^{-rT} times the sum of payoffs weighted by risk-neutral path probabilities (binomial coefficients times p*^k (1-p*)^(n-k)).

places.quote: A European option depends only on the terminal payoffs, so its price is also the discounted risk-neutral expectation over the terminal nodes.

requirements.statement: The payoff of a European put with strike K at expiry is max(K - S_T, 0).

places.quote: \text{Put payoff} = (K - S_T)^+
\text{Put: } (K - S_T)^+ = \max(K - S_T,\,0)

requirements.statement: A lognormal random variable has a normally distributed natural logarithm; if S_t/S_0 ~ LN(mu t, sigma sqrt(t)) then ln(S_t) is normal with mean ln(S_0)+mu t and variance sigma^2 t.

places.quote: The **Lognormal Distribution** $X \sim \text{Lognormal}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ applies when $\ln X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

requirements.statement: For a lognormal stock price model with parameters mu and sigma per year, the log-return over t years has mean mu*t and variance sigma^2*t (parameters scale linearly in time for mean and variance).

resolution.quote: A stock or fund said to follow a lognormal distribution with parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ per year has $\ln(S_t/S_0) \sim N(\mu t, \sigma^2 t)$: the mean and the variance of the log return both grow in proportion to $t$, so its standard deviation grows with $\sqrt t$.
resolution.note: Teaches the per-year lognormal parameter convention, ln(S_t/S_0) ~ N(mu t, sigma^2 t), and its relation to the GBM drift. Source: Haugh, A Brief Introduction to Stochastic Calculus (Columbia IEOR E4706, 2016), §3.2 eq. (13), p.7. Checked by a different agent from the writer.

requirements.statement: Compute a lognormal probability by taking logs of both sides of the inequality, standardizing to a standard normal Z using the mean and standard deviation of ln(S_t), and reading the normal CDF.

places.quote: $$F(x) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$$

requirements.statement: A guaranteed minimum maturity benefit equal to the original investment applies when the fund value at maturity is below the guaranteed amount (it is a put-option-like payoff), and the probability is computed under the real-world distribution with parameter mu, not the risk-free rate.

places.quote: The insurer pays $(G - F_n)^+$ to each survivor, which is a European put on the fund with strike $G$ and expiry $n$.
Each pays $(G - F)^+$ in some form, so each is a put option on the fund

requirements.statement: The initial amount invested in the fund equals the premium net of the expense charge (premium times one minus the expense percentage).

places.quote: $P_t$ is the premium paid at the start of year $t$, of which the fraction $a_t$ is allocated to the fund

resolution.note: the question's own setup: (ii) states the insurer keeps 2.5% and invests the remainder.

requirements.statement: The limited expected value E(X∧u) is the expected value of the loss capped at u, equal to E[min(X,u)] = ∫₀^u x f(x)dx + u[1−F(u)].

places.quote: The **Limited Expected Value** (LEV) of a random variable $X$ at limit $u$ is the expected value of the payment under a policy that pays $X$ up to a maximum of $u$.
For $k = 1$ this is the [[Limited Expected Value|limited expected value]]: integrate $x f(x)$ from $0$ to $u$ and add $u$ times the survival probability $P(X > u)$.

requirements.statement: For a lognormal(μ, σ) loss, E(X∧x) = exp(μ+σ²/2)·Φ((ln x − μ − σ²)/σ) + x[1 − Φ((ln x − μ)/σ)].

places.quote: E[X \wedge d] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln d - \mu - \sigma^2}{\sigma}\right) + d\left[1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln d - \mu}{\sigma}\right)\right]

requirements.statement: For a lognormal loss, the CDF is F(x) = Φ((ln x − μ)/σ), where Φ is the standard normal CDF.

places.quote: F(x) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)

requirements.statement: Expected payment with an ordinary deductible d and policy limit u (maximum covered loss) is E(X∧u) − E(X∧d).

places.quote: E[Y^L] = \alpha\big(E[X \wedge u] - E[X \wedge d]\big)
Y^L = (X \wedge u) - (X \wedge d)

requirements.statement: A policy paying the full loss above a threshold d (up to a cap) can be decomposed into an ordinary deductible d plus a flat bonus of d paid whenever the loss exceeds d, whose expected cost is d·[1−F(d)].

places.quote: Once $X > d$ it pays the whole loss, so with no limit or coinsurance $E[Y^L] = E[(X-d)_+] + d\,S(d)$.

requirements.statement: Under the chain-ladder method, estimated ultimate loss equals cumulative paid loss to date multiplied by the product of all age-to-age development factors after the current development age (including the tail factor to ultimate).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The estimated loss reserve at a given date equals the estimated ultimate loss minus the cumulative claims paid to date.

places.quote: $$\text{Claim reserve} = \text{Ultimate incurred} - \text{Paid to date}$$
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: When actual paid development in the next period equals expected development, the next-period cumulative paid equals current cumulative paid multiplied by the next age-to-age factor, and the ultimate estimate is unchanged.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$f_{n \to n{+}1} = \frac{\text{Losses at age }n{+}1}{\text{Losses at age }n}$$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) development factor is the ratio of cumulative paid loss at one development age to that at the previous age, and the factor to ultimate (tail factor) is the ratio of ultimate loss to cumulative loss at the last observed age.

places.quote: **Development Factor** (link ratio or age-to-age factor) is the ratio used to project cumulative losses from one maturity age to the next, forming the building blocks of the [[Chain Ladder Method]]; chaining them together produces the [[Cumulative Development Factor]] to ultimate.
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Trend each experience year's losses from the midpoint of its accident period to the midpoint of the period during which the new rates will be in effect, using the annual trend rate compounded over that number of years.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + r)^n$$
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: For one-year policies written uniformly over a year, the average accident date of the rate-effective period is one year after the effective date (effective date plus six months for the policy term midpoint plus six months for the average earning lag), so the future period midpoint is one year after the effective date; an accident year's midpoint is July 1 of that year.

places.quote: The first policy is exposed $7/1/2025$–$6/30/2026$ and the last $7/1/2026$–$6/30/2027$, so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: Loss and ALAE ratio for an experience year equals trended ultimate loss and ALAE divided by earned premium at current rate level.

places.quote: The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).
$$\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}$$

requirements.statement: Combine multiple experience years' loss ratios into one projected loss ratio by taking their weighted average using the given credibility/selected weights.

places.quote: Weighting across years in the experience period is a judgment: many companies sum projected losses and premium across all years, which weights each year's loss ratio by its premium; others select weights, often giving more to the most recent years.
Weighting the loss ratios $20/30/50$ toward recency would give $70.9\%$ here, and a slightly lower indication of $+3.9\%$.

requirements.statement: Indicated rate change factor (loss ratio method with fixed expenses) = (projected loss ratio + fixed expense per premium) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit and contingency provision).

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + \text{Fixed Expense Ratio}}{1 - V - Q} - 1$$

requirements.statement: A fixed per-exposure expense (such as a mandated flat commission) is converted to a ratio to premium by dividing it by the current average rate, and is placed in the numerator of the indicated change factor; the variable expenses it replaces (commission %) are removed from the denominator.
requirements.concept: Fixed and Variable Expenses in Ratemaking

places.quote: $F$ enters the **numerator** of the rate; [[Variable Expenses|variable expenses]] $V$ and the profit provision $Q_T$ enter the **denominator**.
Force them to agree — set $F\% = \$25/\$425 = 5.88\%$ — and both give $+3.8\%$.

requirements.statement: New average rate = current average rate × indicated rate change factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: The risk-neutral probability of an up move in a one-period binomial model is q = (S0·e^{rh} − S_d)/(S_u − S_d), where S_u and S_d are the up and down stock prices (with no dividends).

places.quote: $$p^* = \frac{e^{(r - \delta)h} - d}{u - d}$$
$$p^* = \frac{e^{(r-\delta)h} - d}{u - d}$$

requirements.statement: The payoff of a European put option at expiration is max(0, K − S_T), where K is the strike price and S_T is the stock price at expiration.

places.quote: $$\text{Put: } (K - S_T)^+ = \max(K - S_T,\,0)$$

requirements.statement: The option price equals the expected payoff computed under risk-neutral probabilities, discounted at the continuously compounded risk-free rate: price = e^{-rh}[q·payoff_up + (1−q)·payoff_down].

places.quote: $$C = e^{-rh}\left[p^*C_u + (1 - p^*)\,C_d\right]$$
$$V_0 = e^{-rT}\, E^{\mathbb{Q}}\!\left[V_T\right]$$

requirements.statement: The true (real-world) probability of an up move is irrelevant to pricing an option by no-arbitrage or risk-neutral valuation; only the risk-neutral probability is used.

places.quote: The real-world probability of an up move never enters the price, because the replicating portfolio matches the payoff in both states whatever their probabilities are.
The real-world expected return $\alpha$ never enters the price.

requirements.statement: The full credibility standard for limited fluctuation credibility with the observed value within a fraction r of the true value with probability p is lambda_0 = (y_p / r)^2, where y_p is the standard normal percentile at (1+p)/2.

places.quote: $$n_{\text{full}} = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{r}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{[\text{E}(X)]^2}$$
**Frequency**, Poisson: $\sigma_N^2/\mu_N = 1$ and there is no severity term, so the standard reduces to $n_F = (z/k)^2$ expected claims
$$n_{\text{full}} = \left(\frac{z_{(1+p)/2}}{k}\right)^{2}$$

requirements.statement: For average loss per exposure, the number of exposures required for full credibility is n = lambda_0 * (standard deviation / mean)^2, i.e., lambda_0 times the squared coefficient of variation.

places.quote: $$n_{\text{full}} = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}}{r}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{[\text{E}(X)]^2}$$
**Severity**: $n_F = (z/k)^2 \cdot \mathrm{CV}_X^2$ claims, where $\mathrm{CV}_X = \sigma_X/\mu_X$ is the [[Coefficient of Variation]] of claim size

requirements.statement: Partial credibility under limited fluctuation is Z = sqrt(n / n_full), the square root of the ratio of actual exposures to the full credibility standard, capped at 1.

places.quote: $$Z = \min\!\left(1,\, \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}}\right)$$
$$Z = \min\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_F}},\; 1\right)$$
$$Z = \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}} \qquad \text{(limited fluctuation)}$$

requirements.statement: The credibility-weighted premium estimate is Z times the observed experience mean plus (1 - Z) times the prior (collective) mean.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \cdot \bar{X} + (1-Z) \cdot \mu_0$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: The maximum covered loss u is the loss amount above which no additional benefits are paid; with coinsurance α and deductible d, a policy limit L (maximum payment) corresponds to u = L/α + d.
requirements.concept: Policy Limit and Maximum Covered Loss

places.quote: $u$ the **maximum covered loss** (the loss above which the payment stops growing) and $\alpha$ the coinsurance share, so the largest payment is $\alpha(u - d)$.
The policy limit is the largest payment, while the maximum covered loss $u$ is the loss at which the payment stops growing. … and the policy limit is $\alpha(u - d)$

requirements.statement: Expected cost per payment for a policy with deductible d, maximum covered loss u, and coinsurance α is α·[E(X∧u) − E(X∧d)] / [1 − F(d)].
requirements.concept: Expected Payment per Payment with Deductible, Limit and Coinsurance

places.quote: $$E[Y^L] = \alpha\big(E[X \wedge u] - E[X \wedge d]\big)$$ … $$E[Y^P] = \frac{E[Y^L]}{1 - F_X(d)}$$
$$E[Y^P] = \frac{E[X \wedge u] - E[X \wedge d]}{S(d)}$$

requirements.statement: Under uniform inflation of rate r, a Pareto(α, θ) loss becomes Pareto with the same α and θ multiplied by (1+r).

places.quote: A Pareto scales by its $\theta$, so inflated losses are Pareto with $\alpha = 3$, $\theta = 2{,}200$
This is why uniform [[Inflation|inflation]] or a change of currency is handled by changing $\theta$ and nothing else.

requirements.statement: For a Pareto(α, θ) distribution, F(x) = 1 − (θ/(x+θ))^α and E(X∧x) = θ/(α−1)·[1 − (θ/(x+θ))^(α−1)].

places.quote: $$F(x) = 1 - \left(\frac{\theta}{x + \theta}\right)^{\alpha}$$ … $$E[X \wedge x] = \frac{\theta}{\alpha - 1}\left[1 - \left(\frac{\theta}{x + \theta}\right)^{\alpha - 1}\right]$$

requirements.statement: Inflation must be applied to the losses before applying the deductible, limit and coinsurance, with the policy terms held fixed at their stated amounts.
requirements.concept: Effect of Inflation on Deductibles and Limits

places.quote: If losses grow to $(1+r)X$ while $d$ and $u$ stay fixed, deflate the limits instead of inflating the losses
If losses grow to $(1+r)X$ and the limit stays fixed, the expected payment is $(1+r)$ times the limited expected value at the deflated limit $u/(1+r)$.
